Chapter 7: Troubleshooting Setbacks and Plateaus
You know, even when your intentions are strong, it’s completely normal to hit a rough patch or find yourself stuck on a plateau. Life just happens—sometimes you get sick, have to travel, stress piles up, or something unexpected throws off your routine. The mini habit approach is built to handle life’s curveballs, but it’s still good to have a game plan for those moments when things go sideways.
First off, let’s normalize setbacks. Missing a day, or not quite hitting your goal, doesn’t wipe away all the progress you’ve made. What matters most is getting back to your habit as soon as you can—and leaving guilt or self-criticism out of it. There’s a simple mindset that really helps here: “never miss twice.” If you skip a day, just show up the next day, even if you only do the tiniest version of your habit.
Now, what about those plateaus? You know, when it feels like you’re not moving forward or your motivation dips? Sometimes, your mini habit has quietly grown over time and isn’t so “stupid small” anymore. If you notice this, try shrinking your habit back to its original, easy size. That tiny step can help you get your momentum back.
Here are a few quick troubleshooting tips:
First, reassess your minimum. If your habit is starting to feel tough, make it even smaller—seriously, don’t be afraid to lower the bar.
Next, switch up your cue or context. If your old routine just isn’t working, look for a new anchor or trigger to help your habit stick.
Also, take a moment to reflect on your “why.” Reconnect with the deeper reason you wanted to make this change in the first place—it can be a real spark.
And finally, celebrate your streak, not the size of your habit. Consistency matters way more than intensity.
Here’s a real-life example: after traveling for a while, someone struggled to pick up their reading habit again. By going back to their original goal—just reading one page a day—they managed to rebuild their routine without any pressure.
So, remember: setbacks and plateaus aren’t failures. They’re just signals that it’s time to tweak your approach and recommit. The mini habit method is forgiving on purpose—it’s meant to give you flexibility and a fresh start whenever you need one.
